title: The Hours You Can't See
excerpt: The hours that wear owners down are mostly the ones nobody records: the decisions, the replies, and the waiting that no timesheet has a line for.

content.alt: A neatly filled-in weekly timesheet on a wooden desk beside a pile of yellow sticky notes covered in scribbles, with a phone showing a list of unanswered messages lying on top of the pile.
content.credit: The hours on the timesheet, and the ones that never reached it.

content.html: The hours that wear small and medium business owners down are mostly the ones nobody records. A timesheet captures the work that gets handed in: a design, a page of code, a report. It doesn't capture the decision that approved the work, the message that unblocked it, or the two days it sat waiting for someone to say yes. Those hours still get spent. They have no line to land on.

I'll call this unrecorded decision and coordination time: the hours spent deciding, approving, reassigning, answering, and waiting that fall outside any category the business tracks. Each piece is small. A decision takes a few minutes, a reply takes a few more. The cost shows up only when you add them up, and nobody has a reason to add them up.

Imagine you run a 20-person company, and you're the one who makes the calls nobody else can: who moves onto a project when a delivery date shifts, what to charge when the scope changes, whether a client problem goes to you. Say that's about 30 decisions a week, and each one costs you around 15 minutes once you count the thinking and the follow-up. That's seven or eight hours, most of a working day, and none of it shows up anywhere. Your time tracking logs hours against tasks, with no category for coordination, rework, or waiting.

Then picture the queue. At the end of a typical week, a dozen or two items are still waiting on you, and each one takes a few days to clear. Every day an item waits, someone else's work is on hold, and nobody records what that costs either.

If you tried to count all this, you'd probably undercount. You'd be working from memory, because nothing was written down. That's a finding in itself: the business has no way to count its decisions at all.

I saw this firsthand. Early in my career, I contracted at a creative agency where I led a team. I billed my hours to the client by the hour, and the agency could see those. It had no way to see the hours I spent making decisions and managing the team, so the expectations of what else I could deliver assumed those hours didn't exist. I was being asked for more than there was of me, and neither of us could point to where the time had gone.
The company I asked you to imagine isn't invented from nothing. It's drawn from that agency, with the numbers made up and the name left out.
The hours you can see get questioned. Utilization, billable rates, and margin each have a line in a report, so someone asks why they moved. Decision time has no line, so nobody asks.

The load also grows faster than your headcount does. Picture the 10-person version of your company. Ten people can form 45 pairs who might need to coordinate. At 20 people, it's 190. You doubled the team and more than quadrupled the ways it can need to talk to itself. A business takes on a few more people because the work is arriving, and then finds it can't take the next larger deal, because the added hours of managing that work have nowhere to go. In the picture I've drawn, the owner's hours run out before anyone else's do.

If your company's biggest bottleneck is the demand on your time, count the decisions only you can make this week, and how many are waiting on you right now. Multiply the first number by the minutes each one takes, and you have the hours that never reached a timesheet. The second tells you how long other people are waiting on you. A rough count is enough to show whether the load on you is the bottleneck.
